prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a class cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where individual damages questions will overwhelm common questions.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Individualized damages questions defeat predominance under Rule 23(b)(3).**

Rule 23(b)(3) permits certification only if "questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members." Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3). The predominance requirement is demanding. Plaintiffs must prove it by a preponderance of the evidence, and the district court must rigorously analyze the record. *Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811, 815 (7th Cir. 2012). That analysis begins with the elements of the underlying claims. It then asks whether proof of those elements, including injury and damages, can be made through evidence common to the class. *Id.* at 815–17.

**A. Damages are part of the predominance inquiry.**

Plaintiffs may not avoid this inquiry by labeling damages a "remedial" afterthought. The Supreme Court has held that a damages model must measure only the damages attributable to the plaintiffs' theory of liability. If it does not, individual questions overwhelm common ones. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 34–35 (2013). This Court applies the same principle. In *Messner*, it explained that a class may be certified only if the court can fairly conclude that common proof will resolve the contested issues. It also explained that variation among class members in injury and damages bears directly on that conclusion. 669 F.3d at 815–19.

*Pella Corp. v. Saltzman*, 606 F.3d 391 (7th Cir. 2010), shows what happens when it does not. There, the Court reversed certification of a product-defect class. Whether each class member's product was defective, and what each member lost, turned on individual circumstances. *Id.* at 394. A class trial could not fairly resolve those questions with common evidence. *See id.*

**B. Where individual issues dominate, this Court affirms denial of certification.**

This Court has repeatedly upheld the denial of certification when resolving each member's claim would require a separate inquiry into injury or loss. In *Parko v. Shell Oil Co.*, 739 F.3d 1083, 1085 (7th Cir. 2014), the plaintiffs sought to certify a class of property owners affected by a common source of contamination. The Court recognized that a shared source did not make the class claims common. The extent of harm to each property, and the resulting damages, varied from owner to owner. *Id.* In *Chicago Teachers Union, Local No. 1 v. Board of Education*, 797 F.3d 426, 444 (7th Cir. 2015), the Court likewise upheld the denial of certification where the claims turned on facts specific to each class member.

The Court has also said a class is not manageable merely because some common questions exist. In *Carnegie v. Household International, Inc.*, 376 F.3d 656, 661 (7th Cir. 2004), it recognized that individual damages proceedings can be so burdensome that they defeat the efficiency that justifies a class action. *Suchanek v. Sturm Foods, Inc.*, 764 F.3d 750, 760 (7th Cir. 2014), makes the same point. The question is whether the individual inquiries are substantial enough to overwhelm the common ones.

**C. Plaintiffs' authorities do not help them.**

Plaintiffs will cite the principle that individual damages calculations do not by themselves preclude certification. *See, e.g.*, *Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 801 (7th Cir. 2013); *Mullins v. Direct Digital, LLC*, 795 F.3d 654, 671 (7th Cir. 2015). That principle has a limit. It applies when liability can be resolved on a classwide basis and the only individual task left is a mechanical calculation of damages. *See Butler*, 727 F.3d at 801. It does not apply here. Plaintiffs have offered no classwide method for measuring injury or damages. The damages inquiry would require each member to prove that the alleged conduct caused his or her own loss, and to quantify that loss. Those are the kinds of individualized questions that *Comcast*, *Messner*, and *Pella* hold defeat predominance. *See* *Kleen Prods. LLC v. Int'l Paper Co.*, 831 F.3d 919, 922 (7th Cir. 2016) (reviewing certification under the demanding standards of Rule 23(b)(3)).

**D. Conclusion.**

Resolving each class member's claim would require a separate inquiry into injury, causation, and amount of loss. Those inquiries would dwarf any common questions, so the class cannot satisfy Rule 23(b)(3). The Court should reverse the order certifying the class or, in the alternative, vacate it and remand for the district court to apply the correct predominance standard.
